demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
avoid anything that could be stressful
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: I can no longer trust my own body
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: The denial/minimisation in Magical Thinking sits awkwardly with the very global, entrenched negative self-change appraisals. A patient who mainly copes by telling himself the event did not really happen or was not that bad would not typically also report such strongly elaborated identity-collapse appraisals unless there were clearer supporting items linking the trauma to guilt/shame; here the combination feels internally strained.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another', the negative appraisals are missing the expected guilt/responsibility/being dangerous-to-others theme. Instead they focus on global misery and identity change, which is not impossible but is a weak fit to the trauma-specific cognitive content.

vignette:
Miguel is a twenty-two-year-old HVAC technician from a close-knit Latin American family, and for the past fourteen months he has been living in a state he does not recognise as his own. The accident happened on a Tuesday afternoon in late July, when he was on a rooftop performing a routine compressor replacement for a commercial building. His coworker, an older man named Raúl, was on the ground handing up tools. Miguel had the new compressor balanced on the dolly when his grip slipped-his gloves were slick with condensation, or maybe his hand just cramped, he would replay that microsecond a thousand times-and the two-hundred-pound unit tipped over the edge. He heard Raúl shout, then a wet, heavy sound, then a silence that lasted less than a second before the screaming started. The air filled with the sharp, sweet-chemical smell of refrigerant mixed with something metallic and coppery. Raúl survived, but his pelvis was shattered and he spent six weeks in the ICU. Miguel visited him once in the hospital. He could not look at Raúl's wife. He has not visited again.

In the weeks afterward, Miguel could not stop going over the details. He sat on his couch for hours, replaying the identical sequence: the dolly, the tilt, the weight, his hand. He searched for the exact moment he could have done something different-tied a safety rope, waited for help, tightened his grip. Every version ended the same way, but he kept searching. He began to feel that the memory itself was not his own; it was like watching a video of someone else making a mistake, except that someone was also him. Sometimes, without warning, the smell would come back. He would be standing in a client's basement or driving his van, and suddenly the air would go chemical and coppery, and his heart would slam against his ribs, his palms would soak, and he would have to pull over and wait for it to pass. His body had become a traitor. He could no longer trust his hands, his reflexes, his judgment. He was certain that at any moment he could do something catastrophic again.

Silence became a poison. In the quiet between HVAC cycles, in the stillness of his apartment at night, he would freeze, listening for the sound that meant something terrible was about to happen. He learned to keep noise on-television, music, a fan-but even then his muscles stayed tight. He started refusing service calls that felt stressful: anything with a tight deadline, a difficult customer, an unfamiliar rooftop. Then he started calling in sick on days that reminded him of the accident-the anniversary itself, the day Raúl was discharged, the day he first went back to work after the accident. His supervisor noticed. Miguel was given a warning. He quit before they could fire him, telling himself he needed a break. That was eight months ago. Now he lives off savings and the occasional under-the-table repair for neighbors, but only in the apartment complex where he rents, because that is the only place he feels even close to safe. He does not drive his van anymore.

The person he used to be-a reliable young man who helped his mother with the bills, who played soccer on weekends, who laughed easily with his cousins-feels like a stranger. Miguel looks in the mirror and sees someone hollow-eyed and jumpy, someone who cannot forgive himself for not doing more. In his worst moments he replays the scene and imagines himself reaching out and catching the compressor, or shouting a warning a second earlier, and the guilt is a physical weight on his chest. He has begun to believe that he does not deserve to feel safe, that the constant vigilance is a kind of punishment he has earned.

Two weeks ago, his mother found him sitting in the dark at four in the morning, staring at the wall, a fan blowing directly on his face. She made an appointment at the community mental health clinic and told him she would drive him there herself. Miguel agreed because he could not find a reason to say no. He is afraid of what the therapist will think of him, afraid that telling the story out loud will make it more real, but he is more afraid of another night like that one, waiting for a silence that is never really silent.
